notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0128b.stoa015.opp-l: Section 1 is numbered '4' in the scan; this is evidently an error for '1'. In §1 'contumeliis alliceremur' is evidently corrupt; I translate the probable 'contumeliis afficeretur' ('be subjected to insults'). In §3 'in sua severitate' may be an error for 'vanitate' ('vanity'). The sentence beginning 'Quapropter ut Manichaeus...' is garbled: 'utinam victus ex hodierna evangelica lectione' does not construe. I have translated it as a broken wish, which is uncertain. In §4 'ac sic primo carnis animaeque salvatorem' is odd; the reading may be 'proprio' ('his own'), and 'primo' is uncertain. In §5 'totius in latitudine non finitur mentis suae' is probably corrupt, perhaps for 'mundi' ('the breadth of the whole world'); I translate the text as printed. In §6 the citation of Luke 2:28 is corrected to 2:24. Also in §6, 'ecclesiasticae castitatis ... unitatem' probably should read 'caritatis' ('of the Church's love'), which fits the dove imagery. In §7 the editor's '(forte Hi)' ('perhaps Hi') proposes reading 'these' for 'Si'; the sentence is loosely constructed.

Section 2: 'nec te- lis narrationem' read as 'taliter narrationem'; the 'nec' sits awkwardly and the sentence may be corrupt. Section 3: 'vel spiritu' is odd; perhaps 'ne' or 'velut'; rendered by sense. Section 5: 'Mel oculos' is unclear, perhaps 'mentis oculos'; rendered 'the eyes [of the mind]'. Section 1: 'in Pastore' presumably refers to Peter and Rome.

§7: 'unum horam' read as 'unum horum'. §9: the edition's bracketed conjectures 'forte consolationi attentus' (for 'attonitus') and 'forte missione' (for 'jussione') are followed; 'in sancta prædicatione' is odd and may be corrupt. §10: 'anaetatis' is corrupt, probably 'anxietatis' or 'aviditatis', rendered 'longing'; 'Quis ergo etiam hinc videat' makes little sense and is rendered as if 'Quis non...'; 'attoniti' rendered 'intent' consistently with the conjecture in §9. §11: 'dici' read as 'diei'; the sermon ends with an abbreviated doxology.

nodes.text: TWO SERMONS OF ST FULGENTIUS, HITHERTO UNPUBLISHED.
FIRST SERMON.
On the Circumcision of the Lord.

1. The mystery of the divine Incarnation, the excellent sacrament of our reconciliation, is celebrated and honoured by us in the yearly cycle for this reason: that the commemoration of so great a benefit may show what has been bestowed on us, unworthy as we are, and may remind us what we owe to such great glory. Therefore, brothers, the more we have heard that the Lord Jesus Christ was mercifully humbled for us, the more let us acknowledge him as inexpressibly glorious. For in this the only-begotten God plainly showed his unsurpassable love toward us: that for us he took on the humility of true flesh and of true death, not compelled by necessity but moved to pity by goodness. For what good had we done, brothers, that so great a benefit should be granted to us? What good merits of ours were there, that the only-begotten God should deign to become man, that the Most High should be humbled, that the unfailing bread of angels should be suckled at a woman's breasts, that the king of the ages should be subjected to insults, that eternal Life should deign most patiently to die?

2. Consider, then, O man, the condescension of such great kindness, so that you may humbly render thanks. Know, moreover, that you pay not honour but insult to divine grace if you begin to doubt the greatness of so great a benefit. Rather, let us believe without any hesitation that all those things which we have heard about the humility and the humanity of the Lord our Saviour are true. And so let us give the more thanks, brothers, we who, though we deserved punishment, have received grace: by which grace it came about that, while death was justly owed to the lost, life was freely given to the unworthy. For the humility of the most high Saviour brought no loss to him, but conferred a great gain on us; nor did it cast down the exalted, but raised up the cast down. For in order that the Son of God might accomplish the whole work of our redemption, he, the creator of all flesh, not only deigned to be born naturally from the flesh of the Virgin according to the reality of flesh, and, God the maker of man, to become a true man from a human being; but also to be wrapped in swaddling clothes, to be laid in a very narrow manger, to be circumcised on the eighth day, and to be carried to his own temple in human hands. O most merciful kindness of God! O lofty humility of the most high God! He was nursed by his mother as a little infant, who, being boundless, created his mother for himself. He was carried by his parents to his own temple as a little child, who as the great God was entreated by holy men in that same temple. And the same one commanded a sacrifice to be offered for himself, who, being without sin, had come to be sacrificed for our impieties. Consider, then, man, what you owe to the one who is exalted and was humbled for you: to your exalted Creator, to your humbled Redeemer.

3. Nevertheless, dearly beloved, the integrity of the Christian faith has always been accustomed to hold this: that if we read or hear of anything done by Christ according to the canonical narrative of the Evangelists, we should first believe without doubt that the history is true, and then also seek a spiritual understanding within the historical truth. For when the text of the divine history is believed to be true, the Manichaean is confounded in his severity: for, since he does not believe in the reality of the flesh in Christ the Son of God, he strives to lay the charge of falsehood on the holy Scriptures, both old and new. For the wretch curses the divine history of the Old Testament, and in the New Testament he surely denies himself the remedy. For he will not believe that human flesh was formed by God, nor that the circumcision of the flesh was commanded by God to our holy fathers, nor that a victim from the flesh of animals was sacrificed in ancient times to the living and true God, nor that the sabbath was kept by God's command and will, nor that the temple was built for the Lord at God's bidding. And so, since he does not distinguish in the holy Scriptures the character of the times, he spurns and despises the most saving truth of the Lord's Incarnation. Therefore, so that the Manichaean may be overcome and converted by most evident reasoning, would that, overcome by today's Gospel reading, [he might be]! Let us defend the truth of the Old Testament, so that from this we may most plainly prove that the God of the Old and of the New is one!

4. See, from the narrative of the holy Gospel we have learned that Christ the Son of God was truly circumcised, [and] that for Christ the Son of God a sacrifice of flesh was offered, according to the custom of the divine ordinance at that time: and both the circumcision of the flesh and the rule of fleshly sacrifices are known to have been instituted in the Old Testament. Why then, most beloved, should you not most rightly believe in the Old Testament that man was formed by the hands of God, when in the New Testament, so that man should not perish for ever, the only-begotten God himself became a true man for us? Why should it not be believed that God also commanded circumcision to be performed at a fitting time to signify something, when the Son of God had it carried out on his own body? And why should our God not have commanded the Jewish people in past time to offer him figurative victims of flesh, when the only-begotten God himself, born in time from the Jews, deigned to be sacrificed according to the flesh for our sins? Let the Manichaean, then, pay heed to the most manifest and most harmonious truth of both Testaments, and, converted, cast away his own vanity. Let him see in the Old Testament the signifying of things to come, in the New the revealing of things past; and Christ, the God of both Testaments, in the Old Testament promising what he was going to show forth, in the New showing forth what he had promised: neither lying in the promise nor deceitful in the giving; but everywhere good, everywhere just, everywhere holy, everywhere powerful, everywhere merciful: in the Old Testament the most powerful creator of flesh and soul, in the New the most merciful one who took up that same flesh and soul; and thus first the saviour of flesh and soul. Let the Manichaean hear these things, compare them, acknowledge them and believe them, and believing let him return to the Catholic Church, in which he may find the benefit of true salvation.

5. Through these things which the Lord did while placed in the body, he not only deigned to show the harmony of both Testaments, but also wished to shape the conduct of Christians in a saving way: so that what we see was done bodily in him for our salvation, we too may imitate spiritually. For this is why Christ was born a little child on earth: so that the Christian might learn humility. For this reason too he was subject to the parents of his flesh, so that every Christian should always show honour to father and mother. And Christ was wrapped in cheap swaddling clothes so that the Christian should not take delight in costly garments. And Christ chose to appear poor on earth so that rich Christians might learn not to love earthly riches, but by giving alms to the poor might be able to store up their riches in heaven. For this reason Christ was laid in a narrow manger, he who is not bounded by the breadth of the whole of his mind, so that those believing in him might have spiritual fodder, and Christians might learn not to covet the houses or possessions of others. For to what Christian should a house, however cheap, or his own means not be enough, when the narrowness of a small manger was enough for Christ the Son of God?

6. Through the circumcision which the Son of God underwent in the flesh, he foreshowed the circumcision of our heart in the spirit. This circumcision the word of the Law enjoins on us, as Moses says: Circumcise the foreskin of your heart, and be circumcised to your God (Deut. 10:16). With this command the blessed Apostle agrees, saying: For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is that circumcision which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not the letter; whose praise is not from men but from God (Rom. 2:28-29). Therefore Christ had circumcision in the body so that the Christian might have it spiritually in the heart. For this is why he who could have no sin at all put away the foreskin of the flesh: so that we might cast off the desires of wickedness. Christ, then, was carried by hands to the temple, so that the Christian might climb to heaven by good works. Christ wished a sacrifice to be offered for him, so that the Christian might offer himself at the Lord's altar. Above all let him hasten to offer himself by living well. And if he delights to present a clean sacrifice to the divine gaze, we recognise that in the very kind of that sacrifice a certain spiritual sacrifice is also indicated to us: A pair (it says) of turtle-doves, and two young pigeons (Luke 2:24). In this kind of bird, most beloved brothers, a great sacrament of the Catholic faith is commended to you. For in the dove love is recognised, in the turtle-dove chastity is found. For the turtle-dove keeps unstained faith to one mate; and the dove does not desert the unity of the others who live with it. The Catholic Christian, then, truly becomes a spiritual turtle-dove if he keeps the true faith of the Trinity with firm belief, and rejects the mind of heretical wickedness like the defilements of fornication. And he will be a dove if he remains patiently to the end in the Catholic fellowship, and stands firm with unshaken steadfastness against temptations and scandals: so that neither heretical fornication may corrupt the chastity of faith in the heart, nor bitter dissension desert the unity of the Church's chastity. For this is the lawful Church, which keeps faith with the one God as with her lawful husband, and multiplies the gathering of her children in love.

7. In this turtle-dove and dove, most beloved brothers, remain carefully; guard her with all your prayers, so that the Arian may not violate her, nor the Donatist trample her, nor the Manichaean defile her. For these, like evil hawks, long to break up the unity of the dove and desire to violate the chastity of the turtle-dove. For the Manichaean does not believe in true flesh in Christ, the Arian lessens the true divinity in him, and the Donatist breaks up the unity of the Catholic body. The Manichaean does not see the sacrament of the Redeemer, the Arian does not consider the greatness of the Saviour, and the Donatist, like a ravening wolf, has not hesitated to scatter the flock of the Good Shepherd. If therefore, as I said, like evil hawks, wishing to kill the wretched, those eager for vanity or ignorant of the truth, they pursue the love of the dove, curse the chastity of the turtle-dove, and, whomever they can, either devour with the mouth or tear with their claws, then you, most holy brothers, guard the Catholic truth in faith, keep the Catholic peace in love.

8. He offers a sacrifice pleasing to God who, with brotherly love, has kept the true sacrament of the Catholic faith. There one God, one Trinity, is worshipped; neither is the Father proclaimed greater than the Son, nor the Son less than the Father according to divinity; nor is the substance of the Holy Spirit set apart from them, who with the Father and the Son is by nature one God. For the power of the holy Trinity is one, because in three persons there remains one natural substance; the authority is one, because the majesty is one; the eternity is one, because the divinity is one; the lordship over creatures is one, because the making of creation is one. For whatever the Father created, he fashioned through the Son and established in the Holy Spirit. The Son was born of the one who begets; the Holy Spirit proceeds from the one who abides. Yet the Son did not divide the Father by being born, nor did the Spirit lessen God by proceeding, since neither does he increase [him] by inhering. So neither was the Son lessened by being born, nor the Spirit separated by proceeding. For that blessed Trinity itself abides, because there a substantial unity abides; and since nothing in the divinity of the Trinity is created, for that reason nothing there is in any way separated.

9. Hold these things faithfully, most beloved brothers; remain in them constantly. Let this be the thought in your heart and the confession on your lips. Hold the faith which you received in the name of the Trinity. Keep the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace, both of the turtle-dove and of the dove, so that you may always be spiritual in the house of God. May he deign to grant this, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Son.
SERMON II (as it is found in the manuscript, though with a doubtful title).
On the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

1. If the festival of this day is carefully weighed by the faithful, they will undertake to celebrate it with the same devout affection with which they have kept the solemnities of the Lord's Nativity, Circumcision and Epiphany. For this solemnity belongs to the same one as those do, and it is no less than they are. This we shall show in this sermon with clear proofs. Indeed, the solemnity of this day, while unknown to some Christians, is held by many in greater honour than the other solemnities of the year. Above all in that place where the Catholic Church obtained its primacy in the Shepherd, it is held by them in such reverence that on that day the whole crowd of the city gathers together and, gleaming with countless lights of candles, celebrates the solemnities of the Mass; and no one enters the public station who does not hold a light in his hand: as if, that is, they were about to offer the Lord in the temple, or rather to receive him, and so show outwardly by the devotion of their offering the light of faith with which they shine within. For today, in accordance with the law and the gospel, when forty days had passed since the Nativity of Christ, the same Lord was presented in the temple by his parents. Today he was received by holy Simeon and offered to the Father with sacred gifts. Today he is publicly proclaimed by the same Simeon and by Anna to those awaiting the redemption of Israel. O what a holy spectacle, in which only the holy are shown to take delight! On this side stands a virgin and a mother, not of just anyone, but of God; on this side is received the little son of the virgin, whose divinity the world does not contain. Prophets come to meet him from both sides, and both sexes prophesy about the child. An offering is made for the child, not one that might cleanse sins, but one that might declare sacraments.

2. And since I desire to exalt the praise of this day, I would like to run through, by way of discussion, the Gospel reading itself in which I find these things narrated, so that it may answer to what I say; or rather, that the voice of my exhortation may answer to what it narrates. Luke the evangelist, then, setting out the true history of Christ's incarnation more fully and in better order than the other evangelists, after his annunciation made by the angel, after his birth declared by the voices of angels, after the circumcision of the eighth day in his parents' house, follows on in order with these things, saying: After the days of his mother's purification were fulfilled according to the law of Moses, they took him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, as it is written in the law of the Lord: Every male opening the womb shall be called holy to the Lord (Luke 2:22-23). It is clear to all the faithful that the Redeemer's mother in no way contracted a stain from his birth, of which she would be purified by keeping away from the sacred buildings for those days. For without human desire, without any corruption of the flesh, she gave birth as a virgin, and remained a virgin without end; and therefore no male born of her opened her womb. But the evangelist, weaving the narrative in this way, closes the sacrament of the divine incarnation to the impious, and brings in the mother observing the law. Nor is it surprising if the mother observed the law which her Son had come not to abolish but to fulfil. For she knew in what manner she had conceived and who it was she had borne. But observing the common law, she waited for the day of purification and concealed the majesty of her son. This is why, finding him in the temple at twelve years old, she calls him the son of Joseph, saying: Son, why have you done this to us? See, your father and I have been looking for you in sorrow (ibid. 48). Yet she knew beyond doubt that she had conceived him without intercourse with Joseph and brought him forth without virginal corruption.

3. But why did she hide the sacrament of the conception and birth of him whom she knew to be the infinite God? Did she begrudge to others the one whom she carried to the temple and handed into the arms of the holy old man? Far from it. But rather, filled with the spirit of prophecy, [she acted] so as not to reveal the redemption of the world to the impious. For already then, full of grace, inspired by the spirit of the Godhead, she knew that if the princes of this world had recognised him, they would never have crucified him for our salvation. Offer, then, most blessed Virgin, as one observing the law, the one you brought forth, in the temple, so that it may be revealed not to all, but to a few, who it is that you have borne. Let the humble stone cut from the mountain without hands appear for a time, so that it may be rejected by the builders, until, striking the statue on its feet, it grows into a great mountain and fills the whole world.

4. O how small, O how great is the one you have borne! Small in humanity, great in divinity; small in the kingdom of the Jews, great in the kingdom of the gentiles. But he is not thought small by all in the kingdom of the Jews. For you yourself, who bore him, grew as a rod out of that very people of Israel. For you rose as a rod from the root of Jesse and blossomed. As the rod of Aaron you put forth leaves and brought forth a nut; and since above all others you recognised his immensity, though you saw him born of you very small, beyond doubt you adored trembling, and trembled adoring, as almighty God the one you bore as an infant; and yet, because you recognised him as your son according to his humanity, you suckled, cherished and nourished him. Who, do you think, could show us, amid services of this kind, the feeling of your mind, O most blessed Virgin, when on the one hand you saw so tiny an infant born of you, and on the other you considered the infinite God; on the one hand the created, on the other the Creator; on the one hand the weak, on the other the mightiest; on the one hand one to be fed, on the other the one who feeds; on the one hand one not speaking, on the other one teaching the angels? Who, I say, could unlock for us the secrets of your heart, in what ways you turned your thought to both, when, holding in your hands one and the same son of God and of man, on the one hand you adored him as Lord, on the other you kissed him as a little child?

5. Who would not be astounded at so unspeakable a miracle? Who would not become almost speechless? A girl begets her own and all things' Creator, nourishes her own and all things' nourisher, carries to the temple her own and all things' ruler. O wondrous spectacle, at which not only human but also angelic nature is astounded! To this, dearest brothers, lift up the eyes [of the mind]; to this come together with devout affection. There receive Christ humbled in the flesh for you, but adore him as God most high in his divinity. Embrace the little child, but think of the infinite one. Love the humbled one, and fear the most high.

6. Now, most beloved, if it is asked what was mystically signified in our Redeemer's wishing to be carried by his mother and parents from his own city to Jerusalem, to the temple of the Lord, we find that the glorious mother and virgin herself, and her kinsfolk, bore the figure of that Church which believed from among the Jews in the apostles. For when is the Church not a virgin? Her members the Apostle addresses, saying: For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ (2 Cor. 11:2). When is she herself not a mother? For it is said through the Psalmist: Mother Sion will say, A man (Ps. 86:5); and the Lord in the Gospel: Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, sister and mother (Matt. 12:50). When are the elect not kinsfolk, who are called brothers and sisters? So the mother and kinsfolk of our Redeemer carry him from Nazareth to Jerusalem, to the temple of the Lord: because that early Church in the first disciples, driven off by the Jews, brought the dispensation of that same redemption to the knowledge of the gentiles. For that Church, not only from the gentiles but also from the Jews, is rightly called Jerusalem, that is, Vision of peace; of which it is said through the Psalmist: Jerusalem, which is built as a city, whose sharing is in unity (Ps. 121:3). She is also the temple, as it is said to the faithful through Paul: The temple of the Lord is holy, which you are (1 Cor. 3:17). And therefore when the apostles from Judaea, proclaiming Christ, come to the gentiles, Jerusalem indeed comes together with Jerusalem, and temple meets temple, since all these are one city Jerusalem and one temple. In this city, then, and in this temple, Christ offered by the apostles is received. Hence the Church herself also speaks with the voice of the Psalmist, saying: We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple (Ps. 47:10). Understand: in the midst of the Church, which is your temple.

7. But whether according to the history or according to the mystical understanding, the reason why Christ is brought by his parents to the holy city and the temple is made plain when it is added: To give a sacrifice, according to what is said in the law of the Lord, a pair of turtle-doves or two young doves (Luke 2:24). For it had been a precept of the law that whoever happened to lack a lamb, and had found one of these, that is, either a pair of turtle-doves or two young doves, should offer it to God in the offering for a son; and the one who offered either of these, whichever it was, was not to be judged inferior on account of the other. Indeed, in this offering of birds was prefigured that offering which was offered for the salvation of the world in the evening of the day, namely the Lord's passion, through which we have been reconciled to God. For of this sacrifice it is said to the faithful through Paul: Walk in love, as Christ also loved us, and gave himself up for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrance of sweetness (Eph. 5:2); and again: Who loved me, he says, and gave himself up for me (Gal. 2:20).

8. But since all the elect are members of Christ, that is, turtle-doves in the turtle-dove and doves in the dove, this offering of birds also signifies the mortification of the elect, to whom it is said through the same apostle: I beseech you by the mercy of God to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God (Rom. 12:1). But no offering of mortification can be acceptable to God in those in whom there has not been the chastity of true faith and the concord of true chastity. Accordingly it is not without reason that the sacrifice which is reported to have been offered mystically for the Lord is related to have consisted of turtle-doves and doves. For in the turtle-dove chastity is found, and in the dove unity is commended. For the turtle-dove keeps unstained faith to one mate, while the dove does not desert the unity of the others who live with it. The Catholic Christian, therefore, truly becomes a spiritual turtle-dove if he keeps the true faith of the Trinity with firm belief, and rejects the mind of heretical depravity as the defilements of fornication. He will truly be a dove if he remains patiently to the end in the Catholic fellowship, and stands with unmoved firmness against the stumbling-blocks of temptation: so that neither heretical fornication corrupts the chastity of faith in the heart, nor bitter dissension scatters the unity of the Church's chastity. For this is the Catholic Church, which keeps faith to the one Lord as to a lawful husband, and multiplies the gathering of many in the faith.

9. There follows: And behold, there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon; and this man was just and God-fearing, awaiting the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was in him; and he had received an answer from the Holy Spirit that he would not see death unless he saw the Christ of the Lord. And he came in the Spirit into the temple (Luke 2:25–27). Nothing less in holiness is ascribed specially to this man, who is said both to dwell in Jerusalem, that is, in the vision of peace, and to have been just in the working of faith, God-fearing in reverence, intent on the consolation of Israel, filled with the Holy Spirit, and strengthened by his answer concerning the sending of the incarnate Word. O with what burning desire this man waited, according to the promise of the Holy Spirit, to see the Redeemer in the flesh! What do we suppose was the earnestness of his prayer, which deserved to be confirmed by a divine answer concerning the things he was asking? What were the unceasing words of his groanings in holy proclamation? For he did not cease asking until he received an answer concerning the things he was begging for.

10. For in times past there were many inflamed with a like desire, as the Lord attests to the disciples, saying: Many kings and prophets wished to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it (Luke 10:24). But of those, this was granted to him alone who appeared as the last of them in the fullness of time. Yet if with watchful zeal we consider the desire of the saints who followed, for whom to live is Christ and to die is gain (Phil. 1:21), we find that they wished to behold the divinity of the same Saviour with no less ardour of longing than that with which he desired to see him in the flesh. Hence Paul says: I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for that is much better (ibid., 23). Hence the Psalmist says in his own person: My soul has thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God? (Ps. 41:3). Who then does not see from this too that in the one Simeon many, all the elect, are signified through one; who now are found just from faith and works, God-fearing from expectation of what is to come, and intent from the consolation that is to come? In them also the Holy Spirit is known to be present, because it is said through the Apostle: The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5); and again it is said to the faithful: Your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit, whom you have from God (1 Cor. 6:19). And they receive an answer from the Holy Spirit that they will not see death unless they first see the Christ of the Lord: because in this still corruptible life, by the revealing grace of the same Holy Spirit, with the eyes of faith opened, they behold him who promised that he would remain with them to the end of the age (Matt. 28:20), no longer little in the flesh, but infinite in divinity. They also say with the Apostle: Even though we had known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know [him so] (2 Cor. 5:16). These also dwell in Jerusalem, and come in the Spirit into the temple into which Christ is brought. For they themselves are Jerusalem who dwell in Jerusalem; they themselves are also the temple who come into the temple, in whom and by whom Christ is received.

11. We have run through these things briefly, brothers, lest, while we have been eager to show what the mysteries of this day are, and what its holy and pure proclamation is, we become tedious to anyone. There follows: And when his parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him according to the custom of the law, he too took him into his arms, and blessed God, and said: Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace (Luke 2:27–29). Who lives, etc.
